meta.description: Credited to Twain, but unconfirmed: the only source is Gay MacLaren's 1938 memoir, recalling an undated childhood meeting 28 years after his death.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Keep Away from People Who Try to Belittle Your Ambitions'?
meta.ogDescription: Unlike most viral 'Twain' lines this one has a named witness — but nothing in Twain's own hand. It survives only in Gay MacLaren's 1938 memoir.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Twain, and unlike most viral “Twain” lines this one has a named witness behind it — but nothing in Twain’s own hand. Its sole source is Gay MacLaren’s 1938 memoir Morally We Roll Along, which recalls him saying it to her when she was a child; she never dated the meeting, and the words reached print in 1938, twenty-eight years after his death in 1910.

source.heading: The only source there is

source.excerpt: “Little girl,” he said earnestly, “keep away from people who try to belittle your ambitions. Small people always do that, but the really great make you feel that you, too, can become great.”
trail: 1938 — the first appearance. Gay MacLaren’s memoir Morally We Roll Along prints the line on page 66. A scholar obtained the book and photocopied the key pages for Quote Investigator ↗, which knows of no earlier version in any wording.

1938 — the Twain connection is corroborated. Reviewing the memoir, Kirkus ↗ notes that a Lillian Russell impersonation MacLaren performed for Twain gave her an entrée, and that his recommendation put her on the Chautauqua circuit. TIME ↗ reviewed the same book that May, confirming MacLaren as a real Chautauqua performer — though that review does not mention Twain.

1948–1962 — it enters the canon. Caroline Thomas Harnsberger’s Mark Twain at Your Fingertips reprints it in 1948 citing MacLaren’s page 66; newspapers follow in 1952, Dale Carnegie’s Scrapbook in 1959 and Forbes in 1962, all traced by QI ↗.
Today — the provenance mostly falls off. The specialist archive TwainQuotes.com ↗ still carries the MacLaren citation; most quote sites print the line bare, as if Twain had written it.
source.excerptNote: MacLaren places these words at the door, as she was leaving, at the end of a visit she made to Twain as an aspiring child performer. It is her recollection, written down decades later — not a transcript, and not anything Twain himself set down.

source.rightsNote: Twain’s own writings are long in the public domain — but this sentence appears in none of them. The only text that carries it is Gay MacLaren’s Morally We Roll Along (Little, Brown and Company, 1938), and a 1938 book is treated here as in copyright; the Internet Archive’s scan is lending-restricted rather than freely readable, consistent with that. We have not researched whether the book’s US copyright was renewed, so we take the conservative position.

author.name: Mark Twain
author.heading: Who Twain actually was
author.bio: Samuel Langhorne Clemens, writing as Mark Twain, was the most quoted American writer of his century — and, largely because of that fame, the most misquoted. He was also a working lecturer and a generous patron of platform performers, which is how a young elocutionist came to be standing in his doorway at all. The irony of this particular line is that a man who left behind millions of published words is credited with it on the strength of someone else’s memory.

cite.sourceCitation: MacLaren, Gay. Morally We Roll Along. Boston: Little, Brown and Company, 1938, 66. Earliest known appearance of the saying; the attribution to Mark Twain rests on MacLaren's recollection of an undated childhood meeting. See also Quote Investigator, "Quote Origin: Keep Away from People Who Try to Belittle Your Ambitions," March 23, 2013.

copyAttribution: "Keep away from people who try to belittle your ambitions. Small people always do that, but the really great make you feel that you, too, can become great." — attributed to Mark Twain, as recalled in Gay MacLaren, Morally We Roll Along (Boston: Little, Brown and Company, 1938), 66. Twain died in 1910 and never wrote the line himself; MacLaren's memoir, published 1938, is its only source and gives no date for the meeting.

misattribution.heading: What actually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of the wrong person getting the credit — nobody else has ever claimed the line. What goes wrong is subtler: a recollection gets promoted into a citation, and the wording drifts along the way.

items.why: The sentence appears in none of Twain’s books, essays, letters or interviews. Its only source is another author’s memoir, published in 1938 — which Quote Investigator ↗ identifies as the earliest known appearance of any version.

items.who: Mark Twain, on a datable occasion
items.why: MacLaren gave no guidepost dates in her memoir, so the meeting cannot be placed — QI states plainly that the precise date was not clear to it. Any page that assigns this quote a year is inventing one.
A version swapping “people” for “those” and “feel” for “believe” was in circulation by 2003, per QI’s chronology ↗. It does not match the 1938 text.
A St. Albans, Vermont newspaper printed a shortened rewrite — “Small people belittle your ambitions…” — under Twain’s name, documented by QI ↗. A third rearranged variant surfaced in Malta in 2004.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest bottom line: Twain may well have said something very like this to a hopeful child at his door — but the only person who ever reported it wrote it down in 1938 ↗, twenty-eight years after he died, and never said when it happened.

context.heading: The rare Twain quote with a witness
lead: Almost every feel-good line pinned on Mark Twain dissolves when you chase it: no source, no date, no trace before the internet. This one behaves differently. It has a name attached, a page number, and a publisher — page 66 of Morally We Roll Along, the 1938 memoir of the Chautauqua elocutionist Gay Zenola MacLaren, in a chapter she called “I Meet Mark Twain.” A scholar obtained and examined the book and photocopied the key pages for Quote Investigator ↗. The words were spoken, she says, at the door, as she was leaving.

And the relationship was real. Twain genuinely knew and promoted MacLaren: the 1938 Kirkus review ↗ of her memoir notes that an impersonation of Lillian Russell she performed for Twain gave her an entrée, and that it was through his recommendation that she joined the circuit. Quote Investigator also reproduces a 1909 trade-journal advertisement carrying his endorsement of her as “An unusually gifted young lady.” So the encounter is plausible in a way that most apocryphal Twain quotes are not.
detailsBody: Because recalled dialogue is not a document. MacLaren was writing down, decades later, words she says she heard as a child — and she gave no date for the meeting, so there is no way to place it, corroborate it, or check it against Twain’s own papers. Twain died in 1910; the sentence did not reach print until 1938. Nothing in his enormous published output — the books, the essays, the letters, the interviews — contains it.

Quote Investigator closes on a note that cuts both ways: MacLaren was capable of remarkable feats of memory, as her stage act demonstrated. She built a career on memorizing entire plays after a few viewings. That is a genuine reason to take her recollection more seriously than most. It is not the same as evidence, and QI does not present it as such.

From 1938 the line spread through respectable channels rather than dubious ones. Caroline Thomas Harnsberger included it in Mark Twain at Your Fingertips in 1948, citing MacLaren’s page 66 directly. Newspapers in Indiana and Ohio ran it in 1952, Dale Carnegie’s Scrapbook in 1959, Forbes in 1962. The citation dropped away somewhere along the route, which is why the line now circulates as though Twain simply wrote it.
context.pull: A witness, a page number, a publisher — everything except Twain’s own handwriting.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest known appearance is 1938, in Gay Zenola MacLaren's memoir 'Morally We Roll Along', section 'I Meet Mark Twain', page 66, Little, Brown and Company, Boston; QI transcribes the passage ('Little girl,' he said earnestly...), states Twain died in 1910 and the quotation first appeared in a book in 1938, notes MacLaren gave no guidepost dates so the meeting date was unclear, notes she was capable of remarkable feats of memory, and lists the 1948 Harnsberger, 1952 Warsaw Times-Union and Canton Repository, 1959 Dale Carnegie's Scrapbook, 1962 Forbes, 1965 St. Albans Messenger, 2003 'those/believe' and 2004 Malta variants, plus a 1909 Lyceumite ad with Twain's testimonial 'An unusually gifted young lady.'
TwainQuotes.com's Ambition page lists the quote in full and cites it as 'quoted in Morally We Roll Along, by Gay MacLaren (1938)' — in its main quotations directory, not a misattributed list.

The Kirkus review of 'Morally We Roll Along' (publisher Little, Brown) states that a personification of Lillian Russell which MacLaren put on for Mark Twain gave her entrée, and that through his recommendation she became a member of the circuit.
TIME magazine reviewed 'Morally We Roll Along' by Gay MacLaren on 23 May 1938 under the title 'Books: Tent Culture', describing her Chautauqua career; the review itself does not mention Mark Twain.

The Internet Archive holds a scanned copy of 'Morally we roll along' by Gay MacLaren, publisher Little, Brown and Company, dated 1938, flagged access-restricted (lending/print-disabled collections) rather than openly readable.

Wikiquote's Mark Twain page does not contain the word 'belittle' anywhere — the quote appears in neither its sourced nor its misattributed sections (verified by grepping the full raw wikitext, 0 matches).
